questions.title: How does 'de novo' review of summary judgment coexist with agency deference in FOIA Exemption 7(A) cases?
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the court's reasoning in Paragraph III. It states that we review the grant of summary judgment 'de novo', but then says the FBI's decision is entitled to 'deference.' If the court reviews it de novo, aren't they supposed to decide the issue themselves? Does the term 'deference' mean the court only checks for bad faith or frivolousness, or does it actually defer to the FBI's 'law enforcement' determination?

questions.title: Does an 'updated' affidavit cure the defect of a declaration being too 'stale' due to the passage of time?
questions.question_body: In Paragraph II, the district court initially denied the FBI's motion because the Hardy declaration was 'stale' given the time passage. But when the FBI renewed the motion with Bender, the court allowed it. Does the government need to prove that a *new* proceeding was started, or is a declaration simply updating the status of an old proceeding enough to satisfy the 'pending or reasonably anticipated' standard without fresh investigation details?

questions.title: What constitutes a legally sufficient 'segregation' defense under the *Mead Data Center* standard?
questions.question_body: Paragraph V mentions that if non-exempt material is 'interspersed line-by-line' or 'inextricably intertwined,' the agency can withhold the whole record. But how does a court objectively determine this without seeing the actual non-exempt parts? If 1% of a document is public domain, does the *Mead* test require that 1% to be released, or is the burden on the agency to explain why 'meaningful information' cannot be separated?

questions.title: How does the D.C. Circuit define 'interference' with a law enforcement proceeding in Exemption 7(A) cases?
questions.question_body: The court cites *CREW* for requiring 'tipping off' targets as a justifiable reason for withholding. Beyond just 'tipping off' suspects, does the court require evidence that the investigation will *collapse* if the information is released? Or does the mere possibility that evidence might be discovered by a person of interest work without showing that it would terminate the specific enforcement proceedings?

questions.title: Can an appellate court allow reliance on ex parte declarations if the plaintiff never objected to their admission in the district court?
questions.question_body: Paragraph V states that Farahi 'did not oppose the district court's acceptance of ex parte declarations,' so he cannot challenge the reliance. But I don't understand why he didn't oppose it on appeal. Is this a forfeiture rule where FOIA plaintiffs cannot object to secret evidence unless they explicitly do so at the district court stage? If so, does that deprive the plaintiff of Article III standing to challenge the underlying withholding?

questions.title: What agreement is required when an agency uses a 'catch-all' category to withhold documents under FOIA?
questions.question_body: The court notes Farahi 'forfeited' his arguments on categorization because he didn't explain why the categories were overbroad. But if the agency used broad categories to aggregate documents (like 'agent emails' or 'investigative reports') for Exemption 7(A), isn't the court required to verify that the category accurately reflects the content of every document? Why does a plaintiff have to propose more specific categories when the agency is trying to minimize disclosure?
